# On Desire

I had a small meditation yesterday on the ecology of goals. Here’s a tldr:

Any theory of goal-directed agents needs an account of where goals come from, and the optimization frame alone doesn't supply one. Stipulating a goal, like maximizing paperclips, skips the question of how a mind gets from bare existence to wanting anything. In the only goal-directed beings we know, goals bootstrap from innate drives (feeding, sex, play, energy minimization) through behavioral history, so today's goals grow out of yesterday's actions. Goals are therefore path-dependent and shaped by environment. What AIs come to want will follow from what we ask of them now, not from a blank slate.

I want to develop the idea further by getting into desire, which I think is undertheorized, and critical to understand in order to get to a cogent theory of post-AI work. The thing is, most people conflate work with generating a *supply* of something for which there is demand, and miss the point that generating *demand* is work too. Often harder work. Possibly we underestimate this because it’s mostly women who generate, express, and pursue economic demand (there’s a lovely Tolstoy story about this called The Kreutzer Sonata, where a manosphere-ish character rants about it). Aggregate demand is nearly always feminine-coded. Crudely put, you could argue that men just want women, and it’s women who know how to want almost everything else. And yes, there’s knowledge and skill there that defines work. Work that could conceivably be the basis of a new model of human labor.

But first, we need a starting point, and BDI is partially a good one:

 The belief-desire-intention architecture, which grew out of Michael Bratman's philosophy of practical reason and was later formalized for software agents, divides an agent into three parts. Beliefs are what the agent takes the world to be like. Desires are the states of affairs it would like to bring about. Intentions are the desires it has actually committed to, which gives it plans to carry out and a reason not to reconsider everything at every step. That commitment is the clever part. But BDI treats desires as a given, a list handed over at startup, and says nothing about where they came from.

What’s missing in this account is where desires might come from. Goals are downstream of desires, and much less important. The easy cases are desires that are innate biological drives (food, safety, sex, absence of pain, minimization of energy expenditure). The difficult case is desire that cannot be reduced trivially to those basic ones. 

How, for example, might you know you prefer vanilla over chocolate icecream? Or that you want to go see the pyramids? Or travel on a starship? Or that you want to rule as dictator over all humans? Or genocide a hated outgroup? 

By definition desires are attitudes towards what you don’t have yet. But also by definition, they must be conceived in terms of things you *do* already have. For example:

1. Mimetic desire in the Girardian sense requires you to already have a *view* of what someone else has. You can want icecream because you see the happy expression on the face of someone eating icecream.
1. You can conceive of possible things you might want by way of symmetries that transform things you do have. A left glove might lead you to want a right glove. Electrons being a solution to equations might make you realize positrons exist and want to create them.
1. Quantitative scaling: You have 1 paperclip and it makes you happy, so you decide you want two paperclips. Going the other way, if you have 1 outgroup neighbor you might want 0. If you are a genocidal dictator and you have 1 million outgroup citizens you might want 0.

The point is, good of bad, sublime or horrifying, *all desire comes from things you know or have, by some sort of scrutable process* The closest we get to “desire from nowhere” is pushing past a frontier of unknown. Like wanting to see the far side of the moon, which you know by symmetry must exist. Or wanting to try a new restaurant you know nothing about. Or if a portal opens up to somewhere else in the universe, wanting to go through it.

Conceiving of the possible in terms of the actual, and deciding to seek it out, is the work of desiring. Then comes the work of practical reasoning — reconciling the desires with beliefs to conclude it is achievable, setting intentions, making plans (which may involve optimization but this is not that important), and acting. Along the way you must check for conflict with existing policies as Bratman calls them, which introduce trade-offs and tensions. For example, “go through portal” potentially conflicts with “stay safe and pain free” so you might have to consider what might be or not be on the other side (monsters, no oxygen), and prepare (take weapons, oxygen) to mitigate the policy risk.

Here there is also a reward loop. When plans are multi-step with partial rewards along the way, a marginal returns curve is revealed which may reshape the desire. Maybe you *don’t* want ice cream for every meal. Maybe 1 trillion paperclips is enough for you. This is important because most goal-directed behavior is actually highly steerable through observing marginal returns effects. Including observing returns achieved by others. We rarely have to one-shot an all-or-nothing huge desire without being able to sample the desirability on a smaller scale.

The one big exception is the prospect of ruin. When you have a debt of $1000 due tomorrow on pain of death, and only have $1, it pays to gamble it on a 1000:1 odds one-shot bet.
